newsitem.title: FRANCE: US-Iran hostility remains despite watershed vote.
newsitem.headline: US-Iran hostility remains despite watershed vote.

text.p: Hostile ties between Iran and the United States remained frozen in place Tuesday with both sides contending that the other must act if there is to be any improvement in relations.

Senior U.S. officials accompanying President Bill Clinton on a visit to Paris continued to insist Tehran must change its policies before it can expect any alteration in the long- standing U.S. campaign to isolate Iran.

"The things that concern us and trouble us about Iran's behaviour in the world need to change for us to think more liberally about Iran's role in the international community," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.
"And there's no evidence that we see of any change in the fundamental policies of that regime," he told reporters.

McCurry spoke after Iran's new moderate president-elect Mohammad Khatami said Washington and not Tehran held the key to any thaw in the icy relations between the Islamic republic and the United States.

"Our relations with the United States will depend on observing changes in their attitude towards us, but unfortunately we have not seen anything," Khatami told his first news conference after winning a landslide victory in last Friday's polls.

Despite the hardline U.S. view, some experts say the election of a relatively moderate cleric as Iran's president should prompt a rethinking of the long-standing U.S. drive to isolate Iran as a "rogue nation."
"It puts a totally new light on the regime," said Kenneth Katzman, a former Central Intelligence Agency analyst who monitors Iran for the Congressional Research Service.

He said Khatami's defeat of a candidate backed by the fundamentalist religious establishment showed Iran's system was becoming more pluralistic, without necessarily straying from its Islamic and revolutionary moorings.

This provided an opportunity for both sides to search for possible improvement in a relationship poisoned since radicals held 52 Americans hostage at the Tehran embassy from 1979 to 1981, several experts said.

Richard Murphy, an assistant secretary of state in 1983-89 who recently led a Council on Foreign Relations task force on Gulf policy, said the administration should respond with new overtures to show it was serious about its oft-stated readiness to reopen a dialogue with Iran.
Other experts said Washington should quit fighting over restitution of Iranian assets frozen during the hostage crisis and just reach a deal.

Asked about this option, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States was not considering trying to quickly resolve the case as a gesture of goodwill toward the new Iranian government.
He said Khatami"voiced their line on the United States. We're waiting for them to change. If they change, then maybe we'll be in a position maybe to do something."
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, also in Paris for the siging of the Russia-NATO security agreement, underscored this view on Monday.

"We consider it important for Iran to support the Middle East peace process, not be involved in creating and possessing weapons of mass destruction and not supporting terrorism," she told reporters, adding: "Everything depends on how the new government deals with those issues."
Khatami said on Tuesday Iran's Islamic republic opposed the Middle East peace process but would not take any action to disrupt it.
Iran rejects Israeli and U.S. accusations it supported Islamic militants opposed to the peace process and says it only gave political support to groups opposed to peace.
The Iran vote was likely to boost pressure on the United States from Europe to prod for new openings and relax efforts to cement an anti-Tehran alliance.
Clinton and French President Jacques Chirac "touched upon" Iran during a meeting on Tuesday but there was no indication France had dropped its support for dialogue with Tehran.
